CHAPTER XXX

Here Gerard made acquaintance with a monk, who had constructed the
great dial in the prior's garden, and a wheel for drawing water, and
a winnowing machine for the grain, etc., and had ever some ingenious
mechanism on hand. He had made several psalteries and two dulcimers, and
was now attempting a set of regalles, or little organ for the choir.

Now Gerard played the humble psaltery a little; but the monk touched
that instrument divinely, and showed him most agreeably what a novice
he was in music. He also illuminated finely, but could not write so
beautifully as Gerard. Comparing their acquirements with the earnestness
and simplicity of an age in which accomplishments implied a true natural
bent, Youth and Age soon became like brothers, and Gerard was pressed
hard to stay that night. He consulted Denys, who assented with a rueful
shrug.

Gerard told his old new friend whither he was going, and described their
late adventures, softening down the bolster.

“Alack!” said the good old man, “I have been a great traveller in my
day, but none molested me.” He then told him to avoid inns; they were
always haunted by rogues and roysterers, whence his soul might take harm
even did his body escape, and to manage each day's journey so as to lie
at some peaceful monastery; then suddenly breaking off and looking as
sharp as a needle at Gerard, he asked him how long since he had been
shriven? Gerard coloured up and replied feebly--

“Better than a fortnight.”

“And thou an exorcist! No wonder perils have overtaken thee. Come, thou
must be assoiled out of hand.”

“Yes, father,” said Gerard, “and with all mine heart;” and was sinking
down to his knees, with his hands joined, but the monk stopped him half
fretfully--

“Not to me! not to me! not to me! I am as full of the world as thou or
any be that lives in't. My whole soul it is in these wooden pipes, and
sorry leathern stops, which shall perish--with them whose minds are
fixed on such like vanities.”

“Dear father,” said Gerard, “they are for the use of the Church, and
surely that sanctifies the pains and labour spent on them?”

“That is just what the devil has been whispering in mine ear this
while,” said the monk, putting one hand behind his back and shaking his
finger half threateningly, half playfully, at Gerard. “He was even so
kind and thoughtful as to mind me that Solomon built the Lord a house
with rare hangings, and that this in him was counted gracious and no
sin. Oh! he can quote Scripture rarely. But I am not so simple a monk
as you think, my lad,” cried the good father, with sudden defiance,
addressing not Gerard but--Vacancy. “This one toy finished, vigils,
fasts, and prayers for me; prayers standing, prayers lying on the chapel
floor, and prayers in a right good tub of cold water.” He nudged Gerard
and winked his eye knowingly. “Nothing he hates and dreads like seeing
us monks at our orisons up to our chins in cold water. For corpus domat
aqua. So now go confess thy little trumpery sins, pardonable in youth
and secularity, and leave me to mine, sweet to me as honey, and to be
expiated in proportion.”

Gerard bowed his head, but could not help saying, “Where shall I find a
confessor more holy and clement?”

“In each of these cells,” replied the monk simply (they were now in the
corridor) “there, go to Brother Anselm, yonder.”

Gerard followed the monk's direction, and made for a cell; but the doors
were pretty close to one another, and it seems he mistook; for just
as he was about to tap, he heard his old friend crying to him in an
agitated whisper, “Nay! nay! nay!” He turned, and there was the monk
at his cell-door, in a strange state of anxiety, going up and down
and beating the air double-handed, like a bottom sawyer. Gerard really
thought the cell he was at must be inhabited by some dangerous wild
beast, if not by that personage whose presence in the convent had been
so distinctly proclaimed. He looked back inquiringly and went on to the
next door. Then his old friend nodded his head rapidly, bursting in a
moment into a comparatively blissful expression of face, and shot back
into his den. He took his hour-glass, turned it, and went to work on his
regalles; and often he looked up, and said to himself, “Well-a-day, the
sands how swift they run when the man is bent over earthly toys.”

Father Anselm was a venerable monk, with an ample head, and a face all
dignity and love. Therefore Gerard in confessing to him, and replying to
his gentle though searching questions, could not help thinking, “Here is
a head!--Oh dear! oh dear! I wonder whether you will let me draw it when
I have done confessing.” And so his own head got confused, and he forgot
a crime or two. However, he did not lower the bolstering this time,
nor was he so uncandid as to detract from the pagan character of the
bolstered.

The penance inflicted was this: he was to enter the convent church, and
prostrating himself, kiss the lowest step of the altar three times;
then kneeling on the floor, to say three paternosters and a credo: “this
done, come back to me on the instant.”

Accordingly, his short mortification performed, Gerard returned, and
found Father Anselm spreading plaster.

“After the soul the body,” said he; “know that I am the chirurgeon here,
for want of a better. This is going on thy leg; to cool it, not to burn
it; the saints forbid.”

During the operation the monastic leech, who had naturally been
interested by the Dusseldorf branch of Gerard's confession, rather sided
with Denys upon “bleeding.” “We Dominicans seldom let blood nowadays;
the lay leeches say 'tis from timidity and want of skill; but, in sooth,
we have long found that simples will cure most of the ills that can
be cured at all. Besides, they never kill in capable hands; and other
remedies slay like thunderbolts. As for the blood, the Vulgate saith
expressly it is the life of a man.' And in medicine or law, as in
divinity, to be wiser than the All-wise is to be a fool. Moreover,
simples are mighty. The little four-footed creature that kills the
poisonous snake, if bitten herself, finds an herb powerful enough to
quell that poison, though stronger and of swifter operation than any
mortal malady; and we, taught by her wisdom, and our own traditions,
still search and try the virtues of those plants the good God hath
strewed this earth with, some to feed men's bodies, some to heal them.
Only in desperate ills we mix heavenly with earthly virtue. We steep
the hair or the bones of some dead saint in the medicine, and thus work
marvellous cures.”

“Think you, father, it is along of the reliques? for Peter a Floris, a
learned leech and no pagan, denies it stoutly.”

“What knows Peter a Floris? And what know I? I take not on me to say
we can command the saints, and will they nill they, can draw corporal
virtue from their blest remains. But I see that the patient drinking
thus in faith is often bettered as by a charm. Doubtless faith in the
recipient is for much in all these cures. But so 'twas ever. A sick
woman, that all the Jewish leeches failed to cure, did but touch
Christ's garment and was healed in a moment. Had she not touched that
sacred piece of cloth she had never been healed. Had she without faith
not touched it only, but worn it to her grave, I trow she had been none
the better for't. But we do ill to search these things too curiously.
All we see around us calls for faith. Have then a little patience.
We shall soon know all. Meantime, I, thy confessor for the nonce, do
strictly forbid thee, on thy soul's health, to hearken learned lay folk
on things religious. Arrogance is their bane; with it they shut heaven's
open door in their own faces. Mind, I say, learned laics. Unlearned ones
have often been my masters in humility, and may be thine. Thy wound is
cared for; in three days 'twill be but a scar. And now God speed thee,
and the saints make thee as good and as happy as thou art thoughtful
and gracious.” Gerard hoped there was no need to part yet, for he was
to dine in the refectory. But Father Anselm told him, with a shade of
regret just perceptible and no more, that he did not leave his cell this
week, being himself in penitence; and with this he took Gerard's head
delicately in both hands, and kissed him on the brow, and almost before
the cell door had closed on him, was back to his pious offices. Gerard
went away chilled to the heart by the isolation of the monastic life,
and saddened too. “Alas!” he thought, “here is a kind face I must never
look to see again on earth; a kind voice gone from mine ear and my heart
for ever. There is nothing but meeting and parting in this sorrowful
world. Well-a-day! well-a-day!” This pensive mood was interrupted by
a young monk who came for him and took him to the refectory; there he
found several monks seated at a table, and Denys standing like a poker,
being examined as to the towns he should pass through: the friars
then clubbed their knowledge, and marked out the route, noting all the
religious houses on or near that road; and this they gave Gerard. Then
supper, and after it the old monk carried Gerard to his cell, and they
had an eager chat, and the friar incidentally revealed the cause of
his pantomime in the corridor. “Ye had well-nigh fallen into Brother
Jerome's clutches. Yon was his cell.”

“Is Father Jerome an ill man, then?”

“An ill man!” and the friar crossed himself; “a saint, an anchorite, the
very pillar of this house! He had sent ye barefoot to Loretto. Nay, I
forgot, y'are bound for Italy; the spiteful old saint upon earth, had
sent ye to Canterbury or Compostella. But Jerome was born old and with
a cowl; Anselm and I were boys once, and wicked beyond anything you
can imagine” (Gerard wore a somewhat incredulous look): “this keeps us
humble more or less, and makes us reasonably lenient to youth and hot
blood.”

Then, at Gerard's earnest request, one more heavenly strain upon the
psalterion, and so to bed, the troubled spirit calmed, and the sore
heart soothed.


I have described in full this day, marked only by contrast, a day that
came like oil on waves after so many passions and perils--because it
must stand in this narrative as the representative of many such days
which now succeeded to it. For our travellers on their weary way
experienced that which most of my readers will find in the longer
journey of life, viz., that stirring events are not evenly distributed
over the whole road, but come by fits and starts, and as it were, in
clusters. To some extent this may be because they draw one another by
links more or less subtle. But there is more in it than that. It happens
so. Life is an intermittent fever. Now all narrators, whether of history
or fiction, are compelled to slur these barren portions of time or else
line trunks. The practice, however, tends to give the unguarded reader
a wrong arithmetical impression, which there is a particular reason
for avoiding in these pages as far as possible. I invite therefore your
intelligence to my aid, and ask you to try and realize that, although
there were no more vivid adventures for a long while, one day's march
succeeded another; one monastery after another fed and lodged them
gratis with a welcome always charitable, sometimes genial; and though
they met no enemy but winter and rough weather, antagonists not always
contemptible, yet they trudged over a much larger tract of territory
than that, their passage through which I have described so minutely. And
so the pair, Gerard bronzed in the face and travel-stained from head to
foot, and Denys with his shoes in tatters, stiff and footsore both of
them, drew near the Burgundian frontier.

[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"What's the matter, master?" said I.

I could not trace its origin through the howling wind, but then I heard the voice—his voice, diminished and frantic—commanding my return.

I obeyed, stepping back over the jagged stone, and found him frozen exactly where I had left him.

"You called me, master?" I asked, testing the word on my tongue.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

In illumination, the monk was skilled, though he lacked the delicate hand required to match Gerard's beauty. As they compared their disparate talents—the earnestness of the young traveler against the seasoned simplicity of the age—it became clear that Youth and Age had found kinship. They were like brothers, bound by a shared reverence for craft, and the pressure to remain was heavy upon Gerard's heart.

He sought counsel from Denys, who assented with a rueful shrug, acknowledging the pull of the moment. Gerard recounted his journey to the old man, softening the edges of his recent trials. "Alack!" sighed the good old man, his eyes clouding with memory. "I have wandered far in my day, yet no shadow ever molested me." He urged Gerard to shun the inns, places teeming with rogues and rioters where the soul could be poisoned even if the body escaped. Instead, he advised finding refuge in the peace of a monastery for every night's rest. Suddenly, his demeanor shifted; he looked at Gerard with the sharp intensity of a needle, asking, "How long hast thou been shriven?"

Gerard flushed, his reply weak and halting. "Better than a fortnight."

"And thou an exorcist!" the monk exclaimed, disbelief coloring his tone. "No wonder peril has hunted thee. Come, thou must be absolved immediately."

"Yes, father," Gerard agreed fervently, sinking to his knees, palms joined in supplication. But the monk halted him, half-fretful. "Not to me! Not to me! Not to me! My soul is as cluttered with the world as any living man's. My entire devotion lies in these wooden pipes and sorry leather stops, instruments that shall perish with those whose minds are fixated on such vanities."

"Dear father," Gerard pleaded gently, "these are for the service of the Church. Surely that sanctifies the pain and labor poured into them?"

"That is precisely what the Devil has been whispering in my ear lately," the monk retorted, placing one hand behind his back and shaking his finger at Gerard with a gesture that was both threatening and playful. "He was so kind, so thoughtful, to remind me that Solomon built the Lord a house adorned with rare hangings, and that this act was deemed gracious and sinless. Oh! He quotes Scripture with remarkable flair. But I am not so simple a monk as you suppose, my lad," he cried, his voice rising in sudden defiance, addressing not Gerard but the empty space beside him. "This one toy finished, vigils, fasts, and prayers await me. Prayers standing, prayers lying on the chapel floor, and prayers submerged in a right good tub of cold water."

He nudged Gerard, winking with conspiratorial knowingness. "Nothing he hates and dreads more than seeing us monks at our orisons, up to our chins in freezing water. *Corpus domat aqua*—the body dwells in water. So now, go confess thy trifling sins, those pardonable errors of youth and secular wandering, and leave me to mine. They are sweet to me as honey, to be expiated in due measure."

Gerard bowed his head, unable to suppress the question, "Where shall I find a confessor more holy and merciful?"

"In each of these cells," the monk replied simply, gesturing down the corridor. "There, seek Brother Anselm, yonder."

Gerard moved toward the indicated cell, but the doors stood in tight succession, and fate seemed to conspire against him. Just as he raised his hand to knock, he heard his old friend cry out in an agitated whisper, "Nay! Nay! Nay!" He spun around to find the monk pacing frantically before his own cell door, beating the air with doubled hands like a man sawing at a phantom log. Gerard feared the room housed some ferocious beast, or perhaps the very personage whose presence in the convent had been so loudly proclaimed. He glanced back, bewildered, and stepped toward the next door.

Then, his old friend nodded vigorously, his face bursting into a blissful expression before he retreated swiftly into his sanctuary. Inside, he seized his hourglass, flipped it, and returned to his regalles. Often, he would pause, gazing upward, murmuring to himself, "Well-a-day, the sands flow so swiftly when the man bends over earthly toys."

Father Anselm awaited him. He was a venerable figure, his ample head crowned with dignity and love. As Gerard confessed, responding to the priest's gentle yet piercing inquiries, he felt a strange mixture of awe and absurdity. "Here is a head!" he thought, panic rising. "Oh dear, oh dear! I wonder if you will allow me to sketch it once the confession is ended." His own mind grew foggy, crimes forgotten in the haze of admiration. Yet, he did not soften his account of the pagan nature of his travels, nor did he diminish the truth of his experiences.

The penance assigned was brief but solemn: Gerard was to enter the convent church, prostrate himself, and kiss the lowest step of the altar three times. Then, kneeling on the floor, he was to recite three Our Fathers and a Creed. Upon completion, he was to return instantly.

True to his word, Gerard performed his short mortification and returned to find Father Anselm mixing plaster. "After the soul comes the body," the monk declared. "Know that I am the surgeon here, lacking a better title. This is for thy leg; to cool it, not to burn it. The saints forbid otherwise."

During the treatment, the monastic leech, having taken a keen interest in the Düsseldorf episode of Gerard's confession, leaned toward Denys's view on "bleeding." "We Dominicans seldom let blood these days," he explained, his voice steady. "The lay leeches claim it stems from timidity and lack of skill, but in truth, we have long discovered that simples cure most ailments that can be cured at all. Furthermore, they never kill in capable hands, whereas other remedies strike like thunderbolts. As for blood, the Vulgate states expressly that it is the life of a man. And in medicine, as in law or divinity, to be wiser than the All-Wise is to be a fool. Moreover, simples are mighty. Consider the little four-legged creature that kills the poisonous snake; if bitten itself, it finds an herb powerful enough to quell that venom, stronger and swifter than any mortal remedy. Taught by her wisdom and our own traditions, we continue to search and test the virtues of the plants God has strewn across this earth—some to feed the body, others to heal it. Only in desperate cases do we mix heavenly with earthly virtue, steeping the hair or bones of departed saints in the medicine to work miracles."

"Do you truly believe it is the relics, father?" Gerard asked. "For Peter a Floris, a learned physician and no pagan, denies it stoutly."

"What does Peter a Floris know? And what do I know?" the monk countered calmly. "I do not presume to claim we can command the saints, nor that they will, regardless of our will, draw corporal virtue from their blessed remains. Yet, I observe that the patient who drinks thus in faith is often improved as by a charm. Doubtless, faith in the recipient plays a vast role in all such cures. Thus it has always been. A sick woman whom all Jewish physicians failed to heal merely touched Christ's garment and was cured in an instant. Had she not touched that sacred cloth, she would never have recovered. If she had worn it to her grave without faith, I suspect she would have been no better. But we do ill to probe these matters too curiously. Everything around us demands faith. Have then a little patience. We shall soon know all. Meanwhile, I, thy confessor for this nonce, strictly forbid thee, under penalty to thy soul's health, to listen to learned laymen on religious matters. Arrogance is their bane; with it, they shut heaven's open door against their own faces. Mark my words: learned laics. The unlearned have often been my masters in humility, and may become thine."

"The wound is tended; in three days it shall be but a scar," the monk concluded warmly. "Now, God speed thee, and may the saints make thee as good and as happy as thou art thoughtful and gracious."

Gerard lingered, hoping to delay departure for the refectory dinner, but Father Anselm, with a shade of regret barely perceptible, informed him he would not leave his cell that week, being himself in penitence.
